name: spdlog
baseline: glog (also Boost.Log 1.54, easylogging++, g2log for async mode)
workload: Time to write 1,000,000 text log lines to a file, synchronous mode with 1, 10 and 100 threads, best of 3 runs; asynchronous mode compared with g2log by time to enqueue 1,000,000 lines.
claimed_speedup: Synchronous, 1 thread: spdlog 0.302s vs glog 1.066s (3.5x, derived from page data), easylogging 0.975s (3.2x, derived), Boost.Log 4.169s (13.8x, derived). 10 threads: 0.968s vs glog 3.032s (3.1x, derived). 100 threads: 0.497s vs glog 1.139s (2.3x, derived). Async mode, 1 thread: 0.216s vs g2log 1.850s (8.6x, derived).
compiler_and_flags: g++ (CXX ?= g++, version not stated) with -march=native -std=c++11 -pthread -O3 -flto -DNDEBUG, from bench/Makefile at tag v0.14.0 (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gabime/spdlog/v0.14.0/bench/Makefile)
stars_or_usage: 29.7k stars; packaged in Debian, Fedora, Homebrew, vcpkg, conan
tradeoffs: Header-only or compiled library with bundled (or external) fmt formatting; async mode uses a bounded queue with block or overrun policy, so overrun can drop messages; no printf-style-only API; larger compile times in header-only mode (README recommends the compiled version).
caveats: The cross-library table exists in the README at tag v0.14.0 (and its bench/ directory with boost, glog, easylogging and g2log programs); the current README only reports spdlog-only numbers (basic_st 5,777,626 msg/sec on the same i7-4770 for 1M iterations) with no competitor columns. Competitor versions are old (Boost.Log 1.54) and the g++ version is unstated. The compared programs write different line formats: spdlog uses the short pattern '[%Y-%b-%d %T.%e]: %v' while glog writes its longer default prefix (severity, time, pid, file:line), so bytes per line differ. The g2log Makefile rule points at the author's local path. The async comparison measures time to enqueue, not time to reach disk. Numbers are many years old.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/gabime/spdlog (README at tag v0.14.0 and bench/ directory)

name: zlog
workload: Log calls per second on the author's laptop, compared with syslog(3) delivering to rsyslogd (workload and message size not stated in the README).
claimed_speedup: 'high-performance, 250'000 logs/second on my laptop, about 1000 times faster than syslog(3) with rsyslogd' (verbatim from the README feature list).
tradeoffs: Pure C, config-file driven (rules, categories, formats), thread-safe and process-safe file rotation, MDC; calling it from C++ needs only the C header; heavier than printf because every call goes through category and rule lookup.
caveats: First-party sentence with no methodology: no CPU, compiler, flags, message size or rsyslogd configuration. The repo ships test/test_press_syslog.c and test/test_press_zlog.c (load generators for the two sides) but no published syslog timing. doc/performence.txt gives only zlog-vs-zlog and zlog-vs-direct-write timings (1 process x 10 threads x 100000 lines, 'time ./test_press_zlog 1 10 100000': v1.1.1 2.334s, v1.1.0 1.107s, v1.0.3 6.349s; direct write(2) test_press_write 1.872s), which suggests about 430k lines/s for v1.1.1 (derived from page data) and no syslog column. The list entry tagged LGPL-2.1-only; the current repo is Apache-2.0 (LICENSE file and source headers), so older releases may carry the older licence.

name: P7Baical (libP7)
baseline: printf() to console and vsprintf() to a memory buffer (stdio analog of std::cerr); not a logging library
workload: Speed test in the P7 manual: messages per second for printing a simple formatted string to a memory buffer, to the console, and as a P7 trace message (saved to a file) on an Intel i7-870.
claimed_speedup: Figure on page 11 of Documentation/P7.pdf (Intel i7-870, 16.03.2015, sink = file): 'Printing speed: P7 trace: 5 210 000 per sec; Buffer: 688 000 per sec; Console: 10 000 per sec' (about 7.6x the buffer print and 520x the console print, derived from page data). Text on page 10: i7-870 sends 50 000 traces per second at 0.5% CPU, max ~3.3 million per second to the network server.
hardware: Intel i7-870 (manual figure dated 16.03.2015); manual also lists Intel E8400 and ARM 926EJ numbers for P7 alone
stars_or_usage: 26 stars (CMake port repo); upstream distribution at baical.net
tradeoffs: Binary trace format needs the Baical server/viewer (or P7 file reader) to read logs; asynchronous delivery through a client-side buffer pool; C, C++, C# and Python clients; LGPL-3.0-or-later; no dependencies.
caveats: No head-to-head against any logging library (the manual never names spdlog, glog or log4cplus); the only baselines are printf and vsprintf. The P7 side is a call-site enqueue into a ring buffer drained by a background thread, so it is not comparable to a synchronous console print. The test source Tests/Speed/Speed.cpp (in the Faramax/libp7-baical mirror) formats 5 arguments for the buffer case but the P7 trace call passes 1 argument, and its console case calls printf with the already formatted buffer as the format string, so it prints the previous line unformatted and without a newline; the 2015 screenshot may predate this version. Compiler and flags are unstated; numbers are first-party and from 2015. The upstream site baical.net was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so only the GitHub copies of the manual and source were read; the CMakePorts port's last commit was 2020-02-06 (v5.2.0) while upstream may have newer releases. Claim words on the list ('high-speed', 'minimal CPU and memory') match the manual's speed chapter.
